column2: The singular command separates land, kindred and father's household before identifying the land God will show. All three departure relationships and the prospective destination remain explicit; ordinary your correctly addresses Abram rather than God.

Three divine futures promise nationhood, blessing and a great name; the last clause describes Abram as blessed. Retain shall be blessed rather than replacing the selected adjective with the different proposition be a blessing.

The plural blessers and cursers remain parallel, followed by all the tribes of the earth. The passive blessing in you is preserved without importing a later argument about its mechanism or narrowing tribes to an individual nation.
Abram goes in accordance with the Lord's speech; Lot accompanies him. The age is seventy-five at departure from Harran. The temporal when clause is not reassigned to arrival in Canaan.

Sara, the brother's son Lot, acquired possessions and every acquired soul are separately named. Soul here denotes persons, not immaterial objects. Both departure toward Canaan and arrival in Canaan remain; the source does not identify every acquired person's status.

The journey extends through the land's length to Shechem and the high oak. The Canaanites' contemporary residence is an added narrative clause, not a later conquest claim. The tree's botanical identification remains provisional.

The Lord appears and promises the land to Abram's seed. The altar is explicitly dedicated to the Lord who appeared to him. The collective seed wording is retained without deciding its later theological application.

The mountain is east of Bethel; the camp has Bethel toward the sea and Ai eastward. Sea preserves the source's directional image. Altar building and invocation of the Lord's name remain separate actions.

Departure, journeying and camping form the sequence. The destination is wilderness in the displayed Greek, so a more specific geographic region is not substituted. No indefinite series of additional camps is supplied.

The famine occasions descent to Egypt for temporary residence. The final clause explains the famine's severity in the land. Stay conveys the sojourning infinitive without suggesting that Egypt has become Abram's promised permanent home.

The speech occurs as Abram approaches entry into Egypt. The description concerns Sara's attractive face; Abram and Sara retain their pre-renaming forms. The source's explicit I know is not reduced to a narrator's judgment.

Abram predicts the Egyptians' recognition, their identification of Sara as his wife, his killing and her preservation. The contrast between me and you survives. The statement is his feared scenario rather than an independently endorsed forecast.

Abram directs Sara to identify herself as his sister for his welfare and survival. His soul living expresses personal survival here; retaining soul does not justify adding a separate claim about an afterlife.

Entry into Egypt and the Egyptians' perception of Sara's great beauty are retained. The Greek participial transition continues into the officials' actions in the next unit; the English full sentence clarifies narration without omitting that connection.

Pharaoh's officials see, commend and bring Sara into his household. They are the explicit plural agents; the verse does not itself report consummation or say that Pharaoh personally conducted each action.

The source retains plural agents who treat Abram well. Sheep, calves, donkeys, male and female slaves, mules and camels are kept distinct; familiar alternative livestock lists are not substituted for the displayed Greek.

God afflicts Pharaoh and his household because of Sara. The cognate afflict/afflictions wording and both great and grievous qualifiers are preserved. The verse does not specify a medical diagnosis for the afflictions.

Pharaoh summons Abram and confronts what he has done and his failure to disclose the marriage. Rendering the causal question as Why did you not tell me makes its force audible while retaining the source's two linked complaints.

Propose separating Pharaoh's question from the coordinated statement that he took Sara as wife. The source's simple and does not require the inherited so that, which may imply Abram intended that result. The visible wife, taking her and urgent departure remain.

Pharaoh orders men concerning Abram's escort, with wife, possessions and Lot. Lot's explicit presence is retained. The infinitive is the commanded action, not evidence of an independently described expulsion mechanism or armed guard.

The ascent from Egypt includes Abram, his wife, his belongings and Lot, ending in the wilderness. The ordering of the English destination does not remove any member of the departing group or replace wilderness with an imported place name.
Abram's great wealth consists of livestock, silver and gold. The three categories remain distinct; rich is not spiritualized, and no value in modern currency is supplied.

The journey retraces his route toward Bethel and the former tent site between Bethel and Ai. The inherited English makes the return explicit from where he had come while retaining the wilderness phrase and verse-spanning syntax.

The destination is the original altar site, where Abram again invokes the Lord's name. Again is not inserted in the candidate because the return is already expressed by the first-time and former-site relationships.
Lot, identified as Abram's traveling companion, also has sheep, cattle and tents. The possessions belong to Lot rather than Abram; tents are retained alongside livestock as a distinct category.

The land cannot accommodate their living together because of numerous possessions. Both statements of inability to live together are kept; the repetition explains the practical pressure rather than claiming a new moral prohibition.

The dispute is between the two groups of livestock herdsmen. The Canaanites and Perizzites are separately identified as contemporary inhabitants. The verse does not say that these inhabitants caused the dispute.

Abram prohibits strife between the principals and their herdsmen because they are brothers. Brothers retains the Greek kinship idiom despite their uncle-nephew relationship; it is not a change in genealogy.

The question presents the whole land, followed by separation and reciprocal left/right choices. English supplies go for the elliptical directional clauses. The alternatives remain symmetrical and leave Lot the initial choice.

Lot sees the whole irrigated Jordan region before the overthrow. The comparisons with God's garden and Egypt and the limit toward Zoar remain. Their geographic attachment is not converted into a precise map claim.

Lot chooses the whole Jordan district and departs from the east in the selected Greek. That direction is retained even if unfamiliar. The reciprocal separation uses brother as the same kinship idiom as the preceding appeal.
Abram remains in Canaan while Lot inhabits a city of the surrounding district and camps in Sodom. Singular city and actual in Sodom are kept; the latter is not weakened to merely toward Sodom.

The men of Sodom are described as very wicked and sinful before God. The two evaluative terms remain distinct. This verse does not itself enumerate particular acts or authorize inserting a later list of offenses.

God speaks after Lot's separation and commands Abram to look in four directions. North, south, east and sea retain the selected directional vocabulary; the divine speaker is explicit while the addressee remains ordinary singular you.

The promise covers all the visible land, Abram and his seed, with an enduring time expression. For ever is the inherited English choice; the verse is not used here to settle a modern territorial or theological claim.
The comparison is sand of the earth, repeated in the conditional challenge. The condition links counting the sand with counting the seed. Dust is not substituted for the displayed sand noun.
Abram is commanded to rise and traverse both length and breadth of the land. The future gift supplies the reason. The walking command is not expanded into an unexpressed legal ritual.

Abram relocates his tent to the oak associated with Mamre in Hebron, then builds an altar to the Lord. Singular oak and the location relationship are preserved; detailed botanical or archaeological identification remains outside this record.

The opening situates the war in Amraphel's reign and names Arioch, Chedorlaomer and Thargal. Its Greek case sequence is irregular across the opening, so the inherited verse-spanning syntax remains provisional. King of nations is not replaced by an inferred proper kingdom.

The opposing five kings and their cities remain in source order. The parenthesis identifies Balak with Zoar. Existing English name forms are preserved pending a book-wide name-authority review; no historical identification is claimed from spelling alone.

The collective agreement/assembly is associated with the salt ravine, explicitly identified as the Salt Sea. The candidate retains the geographical gloss without turning it into an independently verified modern location.
Twelve years of service precede rebellion in the thirteenth. The plural subjects belong to the subordinate coalition. Service is not narrowed to a specified tribute system absent from the wording.

The counter-campaign occurs in the fourteenth year. Giants, accompanying strong nations and Ommaeans at Shaveh are distinct targets. The Greek-specific groups remain; familiar alternate ethnonyms are not silently imported.

The campaign continues against Horites in Seir's mountains as far as Paran's terebinth in the wilderness. The tree/place boundary is retained without treating the botanical term as a modern coordinate or replacing it with a different landform.

The return reaches the Spring of Judgment, glossed as Kadesh, then the rulers of Amalek and the Amorites in Hazezon-tamar are struck. Rulers follows the displayed Greek rather than an alternate territorial wording.

The five local kings go out and form battle lines in the salt valley. The sentence intentionally continues into the next unit's opposing list. The repetition of city rulers and the Balak/Zoar identification is not compressed away.
The four opposing kings are named in the displayed order, concluding with four against five. Those numbers count rulers in the coalition, not soldiers or cities in the entire campaign.

The repeated pits expression describes an abundance of bitumen pits. The two kings flee and fall there, while survivors flee to the hills. The wording does not state that both kings died; that inference is avoided.

The selected Greek takes the horses of Sodom and Gomorrah and their food. Horses is retained rather than generalized to all possessions. The collective singular Greek equine expression can naturally be plural in English.
Lot, explicitly Abram's brother's son, and his baggage are taken because he resides in Sodom. The kinship and explanatory residence remain separate from the preceding general spoil statement.

An escaped person reports to Abram, called the man from beyond. Mamre, Eshcol and Aunan are his sworn allies. The difficult appositional Greek around Mamre remains a syntactic review point; Hebrew is not substituted for the selected epithet.

Abram hears that Lot his brother has been captured, counts 318 household-born men and pursues to Dan. Slave status is the inherited contextual rendering of household-born, not a separate Greek noun here. Brother remains a kinship idiom.

Abram and his servants attack at night, strike and pursue to Hobah left of Damascus. Left preserves the source's orientation without silently asserting north. No division into military units is inserted into this Greek reading.

The recovered horses of Sodom, Lot, Lot's belongings, women and people are separately named. Repetition of brought back is preserved. The text is not generalized into recovery of unspecified goods alone.
The king of Sodom meets Abram after his return from defeating the allied kings. Shaveh's valley is glossed as the King's Plain. The temporal parenthesis and meeting location remain distinct.
Melchizedek is king of Salem and priest of God Most High. The plural loaves and wine are retained. Later ritual or christological interpretation is not inserted into the narrative action.

Melchizedek blesses Abram in relation to God Most High, identified as creator of heaven and earth. Created follows the selected Greek verb rather than another tradition's possessive wording. Blessed be is an English rendering of the blessing formula.

God is blessed as the one who delivered Abram's enemies into his power. The subsequent he gave him a tenth leaves its subject and recipient pronominal, as in this clause; contextual identification is not newly inserted as a name.

The Sodom king requests the men while offering Abram the horses. These specific objects remain; persons/goods from another rendering are not imposed. The imperatives and for yourself keep the proposed division clear.
Abram says I will stretch out my hand in the displayed future. It is not changed to I have lifted. God Most High is again called creator; the ensuing oath remains connected across the verse boundary.

The Greek conditional oath idiom expresses refusal even of a thread or sandal fastening. Neither/nor conveys its negative force in English. The stated purpose is to prevent the king's claim of enriching Abram, not a general ban on possessions.
Exceptions are the young men's consumed provisions and the allies' portions. Eshcol, Aunan and Mamre are retained in order; their future receipt is explicitly distinguished from Abram's own refusal.

The Lord's word comes in a vision after the preceding events. I shield you renders an active verb, not a separate shield noun. The future reward and its great degree remain distinct from the present assurance.

The master's address and childless departure are clear, but the household clause is not resolved. The feminine household-born form supports the inherited female-servant reading; the relation of Masek, Damascus and Eliezer remains uncertain. Do not silently replace this with a familiar steward sentence.

Abram explains the lack of seed and prospect of a household-born heir. Inherit from me is an idiomatic rendering of inheriting Abram. The slave identification is contextual; the source's household-born term and kinship contrast require lexical review.

The Lord's voice comes immediately and denies inheritance to this man, contrasting the one who comes from Abram. Both demonstrative references remain. No additional biological detail beyond coming from you is supplied.

God brings Abram outside and commands attention to heaven and counting stars if possible. The repeated counting and ensuing comparison with his seed are preserved. This is a comparison of multitude, not an astronomical estimate.

Abram believes God and it is reckoned to him as righteousness. The passive and its pronouns remain without adding an explicit reckoning agent or defining the full theological meaning of righteousness. Later reception does not determine this clause's translation.

God identifies Himself as the one who brought Abram from the Chaldeans' country to give this land for inheritance. The purpose relationship and land demonstrative are retained; a city name absent from this clause is not inserted.
Abram addresses Master Lord and asks by what he will know he will inherit. How expresses the request for a basis of knowledge. The question is not expanded into a demand for a particular sign.

The heifer, female goat and ram are each three years old; the turtledove and pigeon have no corresponding age here. The candidate preserves this distribution instead of extending the age requirement to the birds.

Abram takes the animals, divides them centrally and sets corresponding parts opposite each other. The birds are explicitly not divided. Pieces is a necessary English contextual object, not a new animal category.

Birds descend upon the bodies and their divided parts, and Abram sits with them in the selected Greek. Sat is not replaced by drove away from familiar versions. The referent of with them and the scene's exact force remain open.

At sunset a trance falls on Abram and a great dark fear follows. Trance reflects the selected altered-state noun, without a medical diagnosis. The Greek historical present of the final falling is naturally narrated in past English.

Know for certain expresses the emphatic cognate construction. The seed's foreign residence is followed by enslavement, mistreatment and humiliation over four hundred years. The unspecified they are not silently replaced by a named people in this verse.

God will judge the nation served, after which the descendants come out here with abundant baggage. Here is explicitly present in the selected text. Baggage is retained rather than inflated into a quantified wealth promise.

Abram is contrasted with his descendants: he will go to his fathers peacefully and be buried at a good old age. The participial burial relation is preserved without adding a location or a detailed afterlife description.

Return is placed in the fourth generation, explained by the Amorites' sins not yet being full. Sins remains plural and yet expresses the present incompletion. The statement is not converted into a numerical prediction beyond the source.

Sunset, a flame, a smoking furnace and plural fire torches appear. The relative pronoun grammatically associates passing between the pieces with the torches; the candidate keeps that link rather than making every listed object the subject.

The Lord makes a covenant that day and promises a future land grant to Abram's seed. I will give follows the displayed future. The Egyptian river and great Euphrates bound the expression without an added modern border map.

The three named groups begin the list attached to the land promise. Kenites, Kenizzites and Kadmonites remain in order. Their appositional relationship to land is not expanded into a separate narrative of conquest.

Hittites, Perizzites and Rephaim continue the list in the selected order. Rephaim is preserved as the inherited group name rather than replaced by the giants rendering used for a different Greek word in chapter 14.

The list closes with Amorites, Canaanites, Hivites, Girgashites and Jebusites. The Hivites are not omitted to match another enumeration. Each repeated connective remains represented in the coordinated English list.

Sara's lack of childbirth to Abram contrasts with her possession of an Egyptian slave woman named Hagar. The candidate identifies status and origin without treating Hagar as a free employee or adding a reason for Sara's childlessness.

Sara attributes prevented childbirth to the Lord and tells Abram to approach Hagar so that he may produce children through her. The Greek purpose verb addresses Abram singular; it is not changed to that I may obtain children.

Sara gives her own Egyptian slave woman as a wife to Abram after his ten years in Canaan. Wife is the actual relationship term here. The chronology concerns Abram's residence, not Hagar's age or length of enslavement.

Abram approaches Hagar, who conceives and perceives her pregnancy; her mistress then loses honor in her sight. The English passive preserves the description without adding a verbal insult or assigning motives beyond the clause.

Sara claims injury by Abram and recalls giving Hagar into his bosom. The feminine participle is retained as Sara's I saw within her speech, rather than silently harmonized to Hagar's seeing. Her appeal for divine judgment remains a wish.

Abram places the slave woman in Sara's power and tells her to act as she pleases. Sara mistreats Hagar, who flees. Afflicted must not be read as harmless inconvenience; the narration supplies no endorsement of the abuse.

A messenger of the Lord finds Hagar by a water spring in the wilderness, further located on the road to Shur. The repeated spring locator is retained. Angel is the inherited rendering; no personal name or physical description is added.

The messenger identifies Hagar through her relationship to Sara and asks both origin and destination. Hagar answers only her flight from her mistress. The unprovided destination is not invented to make the dialogue symmetrical.

The singular commands require returning and humbling herself under her mistress's hands. The ancient power image is preserved rather than generalized into advice for modern victims. Translation of the command is distinct from endorsing the situation.

The messenger speaks in the first person and uses an emphatic multiplication construction. Greatly multiply and too numerous to count express its force. The first-person claim is not silently assigned to a different explicit speaker.

Pregnancy, future childbirth, naming Ishmael and the explanation that the Lord heard Hagar's humiliation are separate clauses. The naming is not replaced by an English etymology. Affliction links to the earlier mistreatment without adding a new cause.

The man is described by a difficult rustic/wild adjective, followed by reciprocal hands against all and residence opposite his brothers. Wild man remains provisional; a wild-donkey metaphor absent from this Greek is not imported. Social and geographic force need specialist review.

Hagar addresses the Lord as the God who looked upon her. The second seeing statement contains an appearing participle with a difficult object relationship. Him and before me are interpretive English supports; the syntax and exact force remain unresolved, not certified by retention.

The well's name continues the difficult seeing expression, then locates it between Kadesh and Barad/Bered. The inherited English name translation is provisional; it must not be treated as a securely parsed sentence or replaced by an untranslated Hebrew name without a decision.

Hagar bears Abram a son and Abram names that son Ishmael. Repeated parental identification and the relative clause remain intact. The narrator's naming report is distinguished from the earlier command given to Hagar.
Abram is eighty-six when Hagar bears Ishmael to him. The repeated Abram/Hagar relationships are retained; the age belongs to Abram alone. No harmonized birth year is calculated or inserted.

At ninety-nine Abram receives the Lord's appearance and the words I am your God. Pleasing conduct and blamelessness are separate commands. An Almighty title or walk metaphor absent from this selected Greek is not supplied.

The divine futures concern placing the covenant between the two parties and multiplying Abram greatly. The repeated between construction is naturally represented once in English. This is promise, not an assertion that the population already exists.

Abram falls on his face and God speaks. The humble action precedes the speech introduced in the next unit. The candidate does not insert a spoken response or identify the posture as a specific later ritual.

The emphatic divine introduction presents the covenant with Abram and his future fatherhood of a multitude of nations. As for Me represents the contrastive topic. Nations remains plural rather than reduced to a single collective.

The change from Abram to Abraham is explicit and grounded in God's having appointed him father of many nations. The perfect is represented by have made; its completed force is not mechanically turned into a completed demographic event.

The source doubles the intensifier, so exceedingly, exceedingly is retained. Increase, becoming nations and kings emerging from Abram remain three distinct promises. The repetition is deliberate even where smoother prose might delete it.

The covenant joins God, Abram and his succeeding seed throughout their generations. The enduring covenant and God's relation to both Abram and descendants remain. Their generations marks the collective seed's plural referent without changing the singular addressee.

All Canaan, where Abram sojourns, is promised to him and his seed as an enduring possession. The closing pronoun is plural: God will be their God. The candidate does not make that final relationship only singular.

Abraham and his succeeding seed are charged to keep the covenant through their generations. Ordinary you remains singular for the direct address, while the explicitly coordinated seed shares the obligation. The name change is carried forward.

The verse shifts from singular covenant-keeping address to plural you in the parties and every male among you. Ordinary English obscures that number shift, so it is recorded here. Circumcision applies to each male, not to the entire collective without distinction.

The plural circumcision command concerns the foreskin's flesh and serves as a covenant sign between God and the addressed group. The passive/reflexive construction is preserved without specifying an operator for each person.

The eighth-day requirement includes household-born and silver-purchased males from outside Abraham's seed. The source alternates plural group address and singular your household/seed. The English maintains the categories without implying all foreign persons automatically belong to that household.

The cognate circumcision expression is emphatic, represented by surely. Both household-born and purchased categories recur, followed by the covenant in plural your flesh. This is not a new numerical or medical specification.

The selected reading explicitly repeats the eighth day before the destruction/exclusion warning. That clause is preserved. The relationship of destroyed from kindred to execution or exclusion remains an interpretation question; the wording is not softened or adjudicated here.

Sara is renamed Sarah. These inherited English forms represent the distinction between the source's single- and double-rho name spellings. The candidate preserves the intentional transition instead of treating the spellings as accidental inconsistency.

God blesses her and gives a child through her, then the pronouns shift to masculine him and from him. The candidate preserves that shift and the nations/kings promises; changing the later pronouns to her would alter this selected reading.

Abraham falls, laughs and speaks within his mind. The questions separately identify a hundred-year-old father and ninety-year-old Sarah. Child is supplied as the intelligible subject of being born, not a new source adjective or title.

Abraham petitions God for this Ishmael to live before Him. Let expresses the imperative wish, and Thee marks direct singular divine address. The verse is not replaced by a general blessing that suppresses Ishmael's explicit identity.

God's affirmative response identifies Sarah's future son, commands the name Isaac and establishes the covenant with him and his succeeding seed. The continuing seed relationship is retained; nothing in this translation erases the separate Ishmael blessing.

The answer about Ishmael distinguishes heard and blessed from future increase and multiplication. The selected Greek says twelve nations, not princes. The final great-nation promise and repeated behold remain visible.

The covenant's specific establishment with Isaac is contrasted with the preceding blessing. Sarah's childbirth is placed at this season in the following year. The candidate does not add a calendar month or exact date.
God finishes speaking and goes up from Abraham. The subject of the departure is explicit. The narrative is not expanded into an account of ascent mechanics or a new location.

Abraham circumcises Ishmael, all household-born and silver-purchased males, every male of the household, on that day. The repeated totalizing categories and conformity to God's speech remain; they are not reduced to Ishmael alone.

Abraham is ninety-nine when he circumcises the flesh of his foreskin. The selected Greek is active here; the candidate preserves that form without inferring more about the procedure than the grammar supplies.

Ishmael's age is thirteen, and the circumcision clause is passive. His distinct age and the grammatical contrast with Abraham's preceding active clause are retained. No additional initiation ceremony is supplied.
Abraham and Ishmael are both circumcised on that same day. The repetition confirms simultaneity with the household action; it is not removed as redundant or turned into a second event.

The closing sentence again includes all household men, household-born and those purchased from foreign nations. Abraham's circumcising them is stated after the fronted list. The candidate retains the breadth without adding unmentioned family members.
God appears beside Mamre's oak while Abraham sits at his tent entrance at midday. The temporal participle belongs to Abraham, not God. The source's God designation and noon setting remain explicit.

Abraham looks up, sees three men standing over/near him, runs from the entrance and bows toward the earth. The three visitors are not given additional names or identities in translation; over him remains a spatial expression rather than an asserted hovering miracle.

The address and possessives are singular, in contrast to the following plural hospitality. Lord can be a deferential or divine address in context; retaining ordinary you avoids silently settling the visitor's identity through an archaic pronoun. The conditional favor and negative request remain.

Water is to be brought, an unspecified plural agent is to wash the visitors' feet, and the visitors are to refresh themselves under the tree. All three constructions remain; the singular address of the preceding verse is not imposed on this plural group.

Abraham offers bread before the visitors continue their journey and explains their turning aside to the servant. The visitors' plural reply authorizes what he said. The candidate does not add heart-strengthening wording absent from the selected Greek.

Abraham hurries to Sarah, then commands haste, kneading of three measures of fine flour and preparation of ember-baked cakes. The measures are not converted to guessed modern volumes. The culinary term remains provisional pending specialist lexical comparison.

Abraham runs to the cattle, selects a tender good calf and gives it to a servant. The final he hurried can refer contextually to the servant but remains pronominal, preserving the narrative's possible subject ambiguity.

The meal comprises the inherited curds rendering, milk and prepared calf; the visitors eat while Abraham stands beside them. Curds versus butter is a lexical question, not a resolved ethnographic finding. The standing host and tree location remain.

The question is introduced by a singular he, unlike the earlier plural visitors' reply. Sarah is identified as Abraham's wife and located inside the tent. The candidate retains the singular speaker without supplying an unexpressed name.

The return promise uses an emphatic returning construction and a seasonal time phrase, followed by Sarah's son. Surely return represents the emphasis. The tent-door listening and behind him location are retained; the precise time idiom remains a review item.

Both Abraham and Sarah are old, advanced in days, and Sarah's female cycle has ceased. The inherited euphemism remains rather than being replaced by a new age estimate. This clause provides narrative grounds for the subsequent question.

Sarah laughs within herself and observes that it has not happened to her up to now and her lord is old. The selected Greek does not explicitly mention pleasure. The unspecified it is retained, and my lord here refers to her husband.

The Lord explicitly questions Sarah's internal laughter, quoting her childbirth question and old age. The quotation is not forced to match the prior verse word for word. Though expresses the contrast between possible birth and her aged condition.

The rhetorical question concerns whether a word/matter is impossible with God, followed by a repeated seasonal return and promised son. Word preserves the selected noun and connection with divine speech without restricting its possible matter sense.

Sarah denies laughing because she is afraid, and the response contradicts that denial. The fear explanation belongs to the narrator. The pronoun capitalization is editorial; the source's subject is not newly named in this clause.

The men rise, look down toward both Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abraham accompanies them as an escort. The dual city reference is retained. The accompanying participle explains his walking with them rather than a separate later journey.

The Lord asks whether to conceal His action from Abraham, explicitly called His servant. The rhetorical question and present action remain; the word servant is not dropped or made into an unexpressed title such as prophet.

The becoming construction is emphatic, expressed as surely become. Abraham's nation is both great and numerous, and blessing in him concerns all earthly nations. The text is not reduced to either numerical growth or blessing alone.

God says He knew Abraham would command his sons and household, who will keep the Lord's ways in righteousness and judgment. Knew follows the displayed past form. The final purpose links this conduct with fulfillment of the divine promises.

The increased cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is distinguished from their exceedingly great sins. The candidate keeps both elements without deciding in the verse whether the cry is the victims' complaint or another type of report.

The descent is for seeing in relation to the cry reaching God. The middle/passive completion verb and its subject are difficult; being brought to an end is retained only provisionally. Sense, agency and the elliptical if not, that I may know require specialist review.

The men turn toward Sodom while Abraham remains standing before the Lord. The contrast keeps the departing group distinct from the continuing exchange. No alternative manuscript arrangement or theological identity claim is silently adopted.

Abraham approaches and asks about shared destruction of righteous and ungodly and their resulting equal treatment. The initial negative with aorist subjunctive can carry prohibitive force; the inherited question is provisional, with Do not destroy recorded as a syntactic alternative needing review.

The fifty-righteous condition is posed twice around the questions of destruction and sparing the whole place. Both the numerical condition and the location within the city remain. The plea does not simply request removal of the fifty.

Abraham emphatically rejects killing righteous with ungodly, repeats the equal-treatment problem and appeals to the Judge of all the earth. The second-person divine address and judgment vocabulary are retained, without replacing the argument with a generalized devotional statement.

The Lord's conditional answer promises to spare the entire place if fifty righteous are found within Sodom. For their sake gives the explicit reason. The place is spared as a whole; the promise is not narrowed to those fifty alone.

Abraham acknowledges beginning to speak to the Lord while describing himself as earth and ashes. Earth follows the selected noun. The self-description is not converted into a claim of moral worthlessness or a source-independent theology of human nature.

Five fewer than fifty produces forty-five, and Abraham asks whether that deficiency entails destruction of the whole city. The emphatic negative response depends on finding forty-five. Neither the arithmetic nor the condition is dropped.

A further speech asks about forty; the reply emphatically denies destruction for the forty's sake. Yet again reflects the added-speaking construction. This remains a new step in the negotiation, not a restatement of forty-five.

The request to speak is elliptical in Greek and is smoothed as a deferential appeal without inserting an explicit anger verb. Thirty is proposed and repeated in the conditional reply. Allow is interpretive English support, not an independently present Greek imperative.

Abraham grounds his next request in his opportunity to speak to the Lord, then proposes twenty. The reply denies destruction for the twenty's sake. The candidate keeps this rationale distinct from the preceding if-I-speak appeal.
The final request specifies speaking once more and proposes ten. The answer preserves the emphatic refusal to destroy for the ten's sake. The verse does not state that ten were actually found.

The Lord departs when His speech to Abraham ends, and Abraham returns to his place. The two subjects and their separate movements remain. No additional divine answer or explanation of the conversation's stopping point is supplied.

Two angels arrive at evening, and Lot rises from Sodom's gate to meet them and bows his face to the ground. The number, time and gate location remain; the narrator now explicitly calls the visitors angels.

Lot addresses the visitors in the plural, offering lodging, foot washing and an early departure. They reject the house in favor of the square. Ordinary plural you avoids treating their plural lordly address as singular divine Thou.

Lot's strong urging leads them into his house. He prepares a drinking feast and unleavened bread, and they eat. Feast with drink keeps the beverage element of the selected noun without adding a named drink or modern meal type.

The gathering precedes lying down and surrounds the house with the city's men, young through old, collectively. The broad narrator's description is retained without a demographic calculation. It identifies the crowd's composition, not an additional action by Lot.

The crowd calls Lot out, asks for the visiting men and demands their removal for sexual intercourse. Lie with conveys the contextual sexual sense without erotic elaboration. The coercive setting is supplied by the narrative, not normalized as consensual hospitality.
Lot exits to the entrance and closes the door behind him. The sequence places him outside while the visitors remain within. The verse does not add a weapon, lock or motive beyond that action.

Lot uses emphatic negative address and calls the men brothers while prohibiting wicked action. Brothers is a form of address here, not a genealogical claim. The prohibition is retained without implying approval of his subsequent proposal.

Lot offers his two sexually inexperienced daughters and asks protection for the men beneath his roof. The source's disturbing proposal is preserved without euphemistic removal, endorsement or invented justification. Roof beams keeps the concrete shelter image.

The crowd rebukes the solitary sojourner's judging, threatens him with greater harm and presses toward breaking the door. The rhetorical judging expression is preserved. More than them contrasts Lot with the visitors rather than reporting harm already completed.

The visitors stretch out their hands, pull Lot inside to themselves and close the house door. The concrete rescue sequence and plural agents are maintained; no separate angelic action is inserted between the clauses.

The men at the entrance are struck with a loss of sight, small to great, and become unable to find the door. Blindness is the inherited functional rendering; the exact nature of the affliction is not medically specified.

The visitors ask about sons-in-law, sons, daughters and anyone else belonging to Lot in the city, then order removal. The questions do not establish the existence of each category. Anyone else preserves the invitation's breadth.

The speakers announce destruction because the cry has risen before the Lord and He sent them to wipe the place out. The Greek present can announce impending action; the inherited future is contextual, not a different agent or event.

Lot speaks to sons-in-law described by the perfect participle as having taken his daughters. Had taken is preserved rather than silently changed to were engaged. Their perception that he is joking remains; the family configuration needs separate interpretation.

At dawn the angels urge Lot to take his wife and two daughters and depart to avoid sharing destruction with the city's lawlessness. The daughters are those he has with him; the text is not harmonized by inventing a family member count beyond this scene.

The selected verb for being troubled is plural; the candidate does not replace it with singular Lot lingered. The angels grasp the hands of Lot, his wife and daughters because the Lord spares him. Each person's hand contact remains.

After bringing them out, the speakers urgently command saving one's own life, no looking back or standing in the region, and flight to the mountain. The emphatic cognate save is represented by the urgent imperative; no extra verse is created from the paragraph break.

Lot speaks to them but uses a singular lord in the petition. The number shift is retained without changing the earlier plural narrative. Ordinary you and lower-case lord leave the addressee's exact identification unresolved rather than forcing divine address.

The petition combines received mercy, magnified righteousness and preservation of life, then inability to reach the mountain before calamity. Righteousness is not silently replaced by a different theological term. The rescue purpose explains the preceding favor.

Lot argues that the nearby city is small and reachable, repeats its smallness as a question and anticipates survival there. Soul shall live conveys personal survival. The repetition remains persuasive speech, not a new quantitative city estimate.

Propose shown you favour for the idiom literally honoring/regarding a face. The context grants Lot's request by sparing the named city; the colon carries that explanatory relation. The face image and literal alternative are retained in this record rather than requiring readers to decode the idiom unaided.

Lot is urged to escape quickly because the speaker cannot act until he enters. The naming of Zoar follows. The candidate does not identify the unnamed subject of called or turn cannot into a general limitation on divine power.
Sunrise and Lot's entry into Zoar are the paired events. Their coordination is retained without a precise elapsed time or extra clause claiming the destruction has already begun.

The Lord rains sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven. Both occurrences of Lord are preserved without collapsing the phrasing or inserting an explanation of divine persons. The compounds and direction remain those of the source.

The overthrow affects the cities, surrounding country, inhabitants and what grows from the earth. The successive all expressions are retained. The verse is not expanded into a claim that every region of the world was destroyed.
Lot's wife looks backward and becomes a pillar of salt. The transformation is stated directly; no naturalistic mechanism or additional motive is invented. Her name is not supplied.

Abraham returns early to the place where he had stood before the Lord. English went supports the destination phrase naturally. The earlier standing location links the scene with his intercession without adding another conversation.

Abraham looks toward both cities and the surrounding land and sees a rising flame like a furnace's vapor. Flame is retained rather than replaced by familiar smoke-only wording. The simile does not identify a particular volcanic event.

During the cities' destruction God remembers Abraham and sends Lot out from the overthrow. Repeated Lord/God designations remain. The narrative explicitly links Lot's rescue with Abraham without adding a causal account beyond remembered and sent out.

Lot leaves Zoar for the mountain with both daughters because he fears staying in Zoar. The repeated residence and companions remain. The cave is stated; its modern location and the reason for his fear are not supplied.

The elder daughter addresses the younger about their father's age and absence of a man to approach them in the customary way. This is her claim, not a narrator's certification of worldwide male extinction. Earth/land scope needs contextual care.

The elder proposes wine, intercourse and raising offspring from their father. The plural hortatory sequence retains the daughters' agency. It is translated as a narrated plan without approval or additional sexual detail.

The father receives wine that night; the elder enters and lies with him, while he is unaware of her lying down and rising. Both limits of his unawareness and the repeated night expression remain. Consent is not inferred from that unawareness.

The next day the elder recounts the prior night and directs the younger's action, repeating the wine plan and offspring purpose. The singular command to the younger remains distinct from the joint plural proposal.

The second night repeats wine and intercourse, now with the younger daughter, and the father's unawareness of lying down and rising. The parallel is retained rather than collapsed into a summary that loses the two-night sequence.

Both daughters conceive by their father. The simple result statement is preserved without adding a medical mechanism, moral verdict or time interval. Its plural subject refers back to the two distinct narrated incidents.

The elder's son is Moab; the naming speech From my father is explicit in the selected Greek. The ancestral link to the Moabites and to this day remain. The explanatory words are not treated as a new etymological discovery.

The younger names her son Amman with the explanation Son of my kindred. This selected name and the Ammanite ancestral reference remain instead of replacement by a familiar alternative. The current inherited transliteration awaits authority-list review.

Abraham moves southward, resides between Kadesh and Shur and sojourns in Gerar. The two residence verbs retain the temporary-resident distinction. No new date or motive is inserted into this movement report.

The Greek explicitly explains Abraham's sister statement by fear of being killed and then reports Abimelech's taking Sarah. This explanatory clause is preserved. The king's sending is not reduced to a direct personal seizure by an unnamed agent.

God addresses Abimelech during nighttime sleep with an impending death warning because Sarah is another man's wife. Are to die conveys the contextual present. The statement is not converted into a report that Abimelech is already dead.

Abimelech has not touched Sarah and asks about destroying an unaware yet righteous nation. Ignorant is retained provisionally in the sense of not knowing the situation, not deficient intelligence. The plea concerns a nation, not only himself.

Abimelech cites the sibling claims by both Abraham and Sarah, then asserts pure heart and righteous hands. The two ethical images remain. His claim is reported speech rather than independent certification of every aspect of his conduct.

God acknowledges the pure-hearted act and says He spared Abimelech from sinning against Him, therefore preventing contact with Sarah. The causal sequence remains. Spared has concrete preventative force here, unlike mere retrospective regret.

Restoration of the wife is commanded because Abraham is a prophet who will pray, with life as the result. The alternative warns of death for Abimelech and all his own. The conditional warning is not omitted in favor of reassurance alone.

Abimelech rises early, gathers all servants and recounts all the words in their ears; all the men greatly fear. The repeated all terms and hearing image are retained. The verse does not yet describe a public decree.

Abimelech asks what Abraham has done to us and whether we sinned against him, then specifies the great sin brought on himself and his kingdom. The plural grievance and singular ruler are distinct; the final unusual-deed accusation remains.

The king asks what Abraham saw that led him to act. The participle can suggest an observation or consideration; the inherited literal question is retained rather than expanded into an unexpressed accusation of deliberate malice.

Abraham reports his own inference that reverence for God was absent and his fear of being killed over his wife. The statement is not adopted as the narrator's proven judgment about Gerar. Reverence conveys the compound religious term contextually.

Abraham claims paternal but not maternal sibling kinship, followed by Sarah's becoming his wife. Both lineage qualifications remain. The verse is not softened into a general relative claim or expanded into an unprovided genealogy.

God brings Abraham from his father's house, and Abraham describes his request to Sarah as righteousness. The future you shall show and recurring-place instruction remain. The ethical label is his characterization, not a new editorial endorsement of deception.

The selected Greek includes a thousand didrachms as well as sheep, calves and male and female slaves before Sarah's return. Each category remains; the coin name is not converted to modern currency or omitted because of the later repeated monetary speech.

Abimelech presents his land before Abraham and permits residence wherever pleasing to him. The direct invitation remains singular to Abraham. The candidate does not infer an unrestricted property transfer or named parcel.

The gift is described to Sarah as honor for her face and for all the women with her, followed by a command about truth in all things. The feminine companions and final imperative remain. The social force of face-honor and the imperative's scope remain unresolved.

Abraham prays; God heals Abimelech, his wife and slave women, and childbirth follows. The coordinated subjects are preserved without implying that the king himself gave birth. The exact distribution of healing and resulting births is contextual rather than medically specified.

The explanation uses an emphatic closing construction and the unusual from outside with every womb in Abimelech's household because of Sarah. Wholly expresses the repetition. From outside remains awkward but provisional; it must not be omitted without a syntax-based decision.
